8 NOVEMBER 2026 · LEE C. STONEHOUSE

The gland inside the frame. Bone secretes osteocalcin, a hormone that reaches the pancreas, muscle and brain, and the signal rises and falls with the mechanical load the skeleton carries.

The Skeleton That Whispers: Bone as an Endocrine Organ and the Hormone Nobody Orders

Ask anyone what bone is for and the answer comes back in structural terms: scaffolding, calcium warehouse, frame for the meat. It is the wrong answer, or at least a century out of date. Over the past two decades a quieter discovery has moved from laboratory curiosity to textbook: bone is a gland. The cells that lay down new bone secrete a hormone into the bloodstream, and that hormone tunes blood sugar, primes muscle for effort, and reaches as far as the brain. The skeleton does not merely hold the body up. It talks to it.

Lee C. Stonehouse has long treated the skeleton as the most under-rated player in midlife performance, and the endocrine story is the reason why. People train muscle and measure body fat, yet the organ that coordinates several of the systems they are chasing sits inside the frame itself, and it responds to a stimulus most programs never provide. Understanding what bone broadcasts, and what makes it broadcast louder, reframes what a training session is actually for.

Osteocalcin is the most abundant non-collagen protein in bone matrix, made by osteoblasts as they construct new tissue. For decades it sat in the clinical margins as a marker of bone formation, ordered by bone clinics and ignored by everyone else. The 2007 discovery that changed its status came from a simple question with a disruptive answer: mice engineered without osteocalcin did not merely have odd bones, they had poor glucose tolerance, impaired insulin secretion and more body fat. Bone, it turned out, was helping to run metabolism from the inside.

The active hormonal form is undercarboxylated osteocalcin, the fraction that has shed a mineral-binding tail and can therefore leave the matrix and act on other organs. Its targets include the insulin-secreting cells of the pancreas, muscle fibres, and neurons in regions involved in memory and stress response. In animal work it has been tied to male fertility and to the acute surge in exercise capacity that follows a rise in circulating osteocalcin. One molecule, one gland, several organs.

The endocrine reading of bone matters most in midlife, because the signal declines with age. Bone formation rates fall, the active hormonal fraction falls with them, and a skeleton that senses no mechanical strain turns its broadcast down further. The decline is not a foregone conclusion. It is a response to a missing stimulus, which means the stimulus can be restored.

The most elegant piece of the physiology is the feed-forward loop between bone and muscle. During hard exercise, muscle releases signals that act on bone and prompt osteoblasts to push osteocalcin into circulation. The rising osteocalcin then feeds back on the muscle fibres themselves, supporting their uptake of nutrients and their capacity to keep contracting. Bone, in this reading, is the accessory gland of the workout: the session asks the muscle to work, the muscle asks the bone for its hormone, and the hormone helps the muscle answer.

The loop explains something midlife exercisers feel but rarely have words for: why complete rest makes everything harder. As bone unloads, the hormonal contribution fades, muscle loses one of its supporting signals, and the whole system drifts down together. The loop also explains why the drill for better bone and the drill for better muscle turn out to be the same drill, which is load.

Bone obeys the same rule as muscle: stimulus in, capability out, silence and decline. Decades of sitting are decades of an unstimulated gland. The age-related fall in the active hormonal fraction has been linked in animal models to loss of muscle mass, and the decline is steeper in skeletons that never see meaningful strain. Walking is real stimulus for cardiovascular purposes, but the bone responds to mechanical strain above what daily life provides: heavier loads, impact, direction changes, the signals that make osteoblasts sit up.

There is a measurement angle too. Total osteocalcin and undercarboxylated osteocalcin appear on laboratory menus, and bone formation markers such as P1NP are standard in bone medicine. In practice these read best as a trend across months, a way to see whether a loading program is moving the formation side, with every result in conversation with a qualified clinician. The hormonal fraction is the more speculative read, the formation markers the more established one.

A single hard session can raise circulating osteocalcin within an hour, which is the acute whisper. The seasonal change, bone density and the hormonal baseline, is built by months of progressive loading, the same way muscle is built. The honest state of the evidence: the feed-forward loop and the metabolic effects are strongly demonstrated in animal models and emerging in humans, and no one should order an osteocalcin test expecting a magic number. What is certain is the stimulus. Mechanical strain is the input the skeleton listens to, and the skeleton is listening.

The wider picture sits across the site: the grip strength biomarker and why the motor system predicts survival, the VO2max number that predicts how well you age, and how to read biological age results without fooling yourself.

For readers within a 10 mile radius of Brighton & Hove city centre, the skeleton gets programmed as the endocrine organ it is: progressive load-bearing work in every block, formation markers tracked alongside the strength numbers, and the bone-muscle loop treated as one system rather than two specialties.

Load heavier than daily life, every week. The stimulus bone responds to is strain above the everyday, so at least two sessions a week should include resistance work at meaningful loads or true impact. The bone does not read intent, it reads force through the skeleton.

Progress the load across months. Bone remodels on a seasonal clock, slower than muscle and slower again than the mirror. Pick one load-bearing number, a lift, a carry, a stair power measure, and let it climb for a season before judging anything. The formation markers, where panels include them, follow the same calendar.

If bone markers are on the panel, read them as a trend. Total osteocalcin and P1NP are the established reads on formation, undercarboxylated osteocalcin the emerging hormonal one. One snapshot means little. Three points across a season, beside a loading program, is a conversation worth having with a qualified clinician.

Yes. Osteoblasts, the cells that build bone, secrete osteocalcin into the bloodstream, and insulin-secreting cells, muscle fibres and neurons carry receptors for it. A tissue that releases a signalling molecule into blood to act on distant organs is an endocrine tissue by any textbook definition, and the skeleton qualifies.

In animal and human research it has been linked to sharper insulin release from the pancreas, better glucose handling in muscle, a boost to acute exercise capacity through muscle feedback, and roles in male fertility and aspects of brain function. The effects are graded, measurable and run in the direction of better metabolic and physical performance.

Bone formation rate declines with age, and undercarboxylated osteocalcin, the active hormonal fraction, falls with it. Long stretches of sitting and decades of minimal mechanical loading accelerate the decline. Bone that senses no strain down-regulates its endocrine output, exactly as unstimulated muscle sheds protein.

A single hard session can raise circulating osteocalcin within an hour, and loading programs raise bone formation markers over weeks to months. The honest caveat is that the hormonal benefits demonstrated so far are strongest in animal models and emerging in humans. What is certain is that mechanical strain is the stimulus the skeleton listens to.

Yes, total osteocalcin and undercarboxylated osteocalcin exist on laboratory menus, and bone formation markers such as P1NP are standard in bone clinics. Results belong in conversation with a qualified clinician, and they are most useful read as a trend across months, next to a strength program and the rest of the panel, not on their own.

The skeleton has been posing as scaffolding when it has been a gland all along. Load it the way it expects to be loaded, watch the formation markers and the strength numbers climb on the same calendar, and let the whisper get louder. The frame is not passive. It never was.

None of it is a guarantee. All of it beats guessing.
